transcript.text: Ebola Update We go behind the scenes at Walter Reed
where scientists are monitoring an experimental vaccine.
Navy History, an F-35C Joint Strike Fighter makes its first arrested landing on an aircraft
carrier.
The Sasebo visit, a U.S. dignitary, stops in Japan to thank sailors.
Welcome to DOD News Now, I'm Sergeant Adam Ross.
And Ebola vaccine is in the works at Walter Reed Army Institute for Research.
39 people were injected with the vaccine and are being closely monitored by doctors.
The vaccine is essentially made from a different virus which researchers have modified to make
the body think it's Ebola.
They've taken that particular virus and they've taken the gene out of it and they've
taken a gene from Ebola.
And in particular it's the gene that makes the coat that the virus likes to wear when
it's circulating in the body.
And they put that gene in the VSV virus.
So I give it to you and it replicates and when it replicates it puts on that coat.
So it looks like Ebola to the body but it's not Ebola.
It doesn't have the ability to cause Ebola and it doesn't cause Ebola disease.
The body reacts to the vaccine by producing antibodies which would fight the real virus.
Researchers hope to have enough data from this trial to move on to the next phase, come December.
Top Navy officials are calling it a historic day for naval aviation.
They're talking about the first arrested landing by an F-35C Joint Strike Fighter on
an aircraft carrier yesterday off the coast of San Diego.
Navy test pilot Commander Tony Wilson landed the F-35 on the flight deck of USS Nimitz and
what officials say is the beginning of about two weeks of at-sea testing for the fighter jet.
Officials say testing will also take place at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland
where aircraft will perform a variety of operational maneuvers including catapult take-offs and arrested
landings.
NASA will also analyze data to measure the F-35's integration into flight deck operations.
Navy officials hope the F-35C will be fully capable and ready to deploy to the fleet in
The United States Ambassador to Japan Caroline Kennedy recently visited Fleet Activities
Sassibo to thank sailors for their service.
Petty Officer Hillary Browning reports.
Often referred to as the Princess of America, Caroline Kennedy is the United States Ambassador
to Japan and part of her role is to help strengthen the bond between Japanese and American military
forces.
She stopped by Fleet Activities Sassibo to meet with the city mayor and to tour the base
and the amphibious assault ship USS Bonhomra Shard.
It's a great honor to share this afternoon with you.
I've heard a great deal about the cooperation between Japan base as well as our base here
at Sassibo and I can see the reality of that as we were touring around the harbor.
So it's a great tribute to everyone here that this cooperation is so close and so supportive.
Ambassador Kennedy says that being in Asia and visiting with sailors is always a special
experience.
It's all who probably know my father served in the US Navy and you're in the Pacific and
so I have a special place in my heart for the men and women of the Navy and it's always
a great, very emotional experience for me to be able to visit the US Navy base and ships.
After her tour she took time to meet with sailors and their families individually.
How are you ma'am?
You've got the sunglasses to meet you.
This is our children.
Children, which of course was a great photo opportunity.
This was the ambassador's first time on board the BHR.
She hopes to visit again as the fleet shifts its focus to the Pacific.
Petty Officer Hillary Browning, fleet activities, Sassibo Japan.
And just a reminder be sure to check out the DoD Facebook page for the latest on the campaign
to take out ISIL.
Watch for us also on Twitter.
I'm Sergeant Adam Ross.
Keep it right here for the latest in DoD News.
